planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in early spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Erecta tolerates heavier, poorly drained soils better than most shrubs and needs little pruning to maintain its narrow, upright shape.

directions: Erecta is a distinctly upright, narrow-growing selection of native red chokeberry, with erect branching that stays tight and columnar rather than spreading wide like the species or the rounded 'Brilliantissima', making it a good choice for narrow screens, foundation plantings, and hedgerows where width is limited. Clusters of small white spring flowers give way to abundant bright red berries that persist well into winter, feeding birds after most other fruit has been stripped from the landscape, while the glossy dark green summer foliage turns strong orange-red in fall. It tolerates wet, heavy soils, part shade, and a wide range of conditions with minimal care, suckering modestly over time to form a narrow colony if left unchecked.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Berry Scape Red Chokeberry (Compact UConn-Bred Fruiting Red Chokeberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Berry Scape is fully branched to the ground from the start, so it needs no corrective pruning to fill in like older, leggier red chokeberry cultivars.

directions: Berry Scape is a compact, densely mounded red chokeberry released through the University of Connecticut's ornamental Aronia breeding program, selected from seedlings for a naturally tight, fully branched habit roughly one-third to one-half the size of the older 'Brilliantissima', with no sparse or leggy lower stems to prune out. White spring flower clusters, red summer-into-fall berries, and red fall foliage all appear noticeably earlier in the season than on standard red chokeberry cultivars, giving an extended, layered display of bloom, fruit, and color on the same compact plant. It shares the straight species' tolerance for wet or heavy soils and needs only minimal maintenance once established, making it well suited to foundation plantings and smaller gardens where full-size red chokeberry would be too large.
sources: HortScience (American Society for Horticultural Science), Vol. 61

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in early spring in average, medium-moisture, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; best fruit set occurs in full sun. Professor Ed stays compact enough for a mixed border or small-space planting without the size of standard melanocarpa cultivars like Viking or Nero.

directions: Professor Ed is a compact black chokeberry cultivar, named in honor of longtime University of Wisconsin horticulture professor Edward Hasselkus, that stays to roughly 3-4 feet tall and wide over its first decade rather than growing into the taller thicket typical of the species. It carries the same ornamental and fruiting traits as wild black chokeberry in miniature: clusters of small white five-petaled flowers in May, glossy dark green summer foliage, blueberry-sized black fall fruit, and purple-red fall color. The berries are tart and astringent fresh but make good jams, jellies, and syrups once cooked or processed, and the plant's small mature size makes it easier to net or harvest than full-size aronia cultivars grown for commercial fruit production.

common_name: Cherry Lace Elderberry (Pink-Flowered Cutleaf Black Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; give afternoon shade in hot climates to help the deep burgundy foliage color hold through summer.

directions: Cherry Lace is a patented ornamental black elderberry discovered as a chance seedling of the popular 'Black Lace' at a Welsh nursery, grown chiefly for its finely dissected, deep burgundy-red foliage and its clusters of pale pink, lightly fragrant flowers, both noticeably pinker and redder than its 'Black Lace' parent. It stays more compact than many black-leaved elderberry cultivars, forming a dense mound of lacy foliage well suited to a mixed border or large container, followed by small dark berries in late summer that provide food for birds. As with other ornamental elderberries, raw berries and other plant parts are mildly toxic and are left for wildlife rather than harvested, and a hard prune in late winter keeps the plant compact and encourages the most vividly colored new growth.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society nursery trade listings
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder (Sambucus nigra cultivar group)
North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in late winter to spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Æ-1 is self-compatible and sets fruit reliably on its own, but a second elderberry cultivar nearby can extend the harvest window.

directions: Æ-1 is a patented American elderberry bred specifically for warm, low-chill climates such as north-central Florida and the Gulf Coast, where standard elderberry cultivars developed in the Midwest and Europe often ripen unevenly or underperform for lack of winter chilling. It requires only a few hundred chill hours, ripens its fruit early and unusually evenly across each cluster over a short harvest window, and sets a reliable, self-compatible crop of medium to medium-large dark berries rich in anthocyanins. The semi-erect shrub stays smaller and more restrained than many American elderberry cultivars, making it a practical option for home gardeners in zone 8-10 who have struggled to get good production from Adams, York, or other northern-bred selections. As with all elderberries, cook the fruit before eating; raw berries and other plant parts contain cyanogenic compounds that are destroyed by heat.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Elderberry

common_name: Black Diamond Elderberry (Long-Storage High-Yield American Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Black Diamond is self-fertile but benefits from a second elderberry cultivar nearby for improved cross-pollination and yield.

directions: Black Diamond is the first named release of a roughly three-decade elderberry breeding program, selected from wild American elderberry parentage for disease resistance, uniform cluster ripening, and rich flavor. Its standout trait is post-harvest storage life: picked berries keep in cold storage for up to about three weeks, nearly twice as long as typical elderberry cultivars, a significant advantage for anyone processing a large harvest over time rather than all at once. Plants reach a moderate 5-8 feet at maturity, smaller than many American elderberry cultivars, with the typical flat-topped white flower clusters in early summer followed by heavy clusters of dark purple-black berries in late summer. Cook all berries before eating or processing into syrup, jam, or wine, since raw elderberries contain cyanogenic compounds that heat destroys.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Albida grows and flowers much like the straight species but is planted specifically for its pale, unusual fruit color.

directions: Albida is an old European black elderberry selection notable for fruit that ripens pale golden-green to creamy white rather than the usual near-black of the species, a curiosity that makes it a talking-point specimen rather than a juice or syrup producer. It otherwise grows and flowers like typical Sambucus nigra, with large, flat-topped clusters of fragrant white flowers in early summer that can be harvested for elderflower cordial, followed by the pale drooping fruit clusters in late summer. Because the unusual coloring has made it uncommon in general cultivation, it is best sourced from specialty or collector nurseries rather than typical garden centers. Prune out a few of the oldest stems each winter to keep the shrub productive, and note that, as with all elderberry, raw fruit should be cooked before any culinary use.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder (Sambucus nigra cultivar group)

common_name: Golden Locks Elderberry (Dwarf Golden Cutleaf European Red Elder)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; give afternoon shade in hot-summer climates to keep the gold foliage from scorching.

directions: Golden Locks is a dwarf, finely dissected selection of European red elder, staying noticeably smaller than sister cutleaf gold cultivars like Sutherland Gold while sharing the same lacy, fern-like texture. New foliage emerges a soft chartreuse-gold and holds color through the season better than many gold-leaved shrubs, given a little afternoon shade in hot climates, with creamy white spring flower clusters followed by bright red berries that are an important early food source for birds. Like other red elderberries, the raw fruit and other plant parts are mildly toxic to people and are best left for wildlife rather than harvested. Prune hard in late winter to renew the most vividly colored foliage on strong new growth.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder (Sambucus racemosa cultivar group)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; David Smith is self-fertile and stays more compact than many white mulberry selections, making it practical for a home orchard.

directions: David Smith is a cold-hardy white mulberry selection, traced to the collection of fruit explorer Richard Fahey, valued for an unusually long harvest season of heavy crops of sweet, medium-sized black-ripening fruit. It is more compact and manageable than many seedling mulberries, generally staying in the 6-12 foot range with pruning, which makes netting against birds and hand harvest easier than on a full-size tree. Mulberries are self-fertile but wind-pollinated, so a second tree nearby can improve fruit set; harvest over several weeks in summer as individual berries along each cluster ripen unevenly, and spread a tarp or sheet beneath the canopy to catch ripe fruit as it drops rather than hand-picking the whole crop.
sources: Growing Fruit forum (citing Richard Fahey collection provenance)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in spring in full sun to partial shade on well-drained soil; Stubbs is self-fertile and vigorous, so allow room for a large, spreading canopy or commit to annual pruning to control size.

directions: Stubbs is a Southern heirloom mulberry dating to around 1870 in Georgia, long grown for its prolific crops of sweet, flavorful fruit even though it is believed to carry some white mulberry (Morus alba) ancestry rather than being a pure red mulberry. It bears heavily over a long early-to-midsummer season, dropping ripe fruit continuously, which makes a tarp or netting beneath the canopy the easiest way to harvest without staining hands and clothing from hand-picking. Left unpruned it grows into a large shade tree, so gardeners wanting an easier home-orchard size should prune annually to maintain a lower, broader canopy. As with other mulberries, fruit ripens unevenly along the cluster, so harvest continues over several weeks rather than all at once.
sources: Growing Fruit forum (mulberry cultivar identification discussion)
North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox (Morus rubra)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in spring in full sun to partial shade on well-drained soil; Johnson is an older, lower-yielding selection best suited to collectors and home orchardists prioritizing large individual fruit over heavy total crop.

directions: Johnson is a long-established named red mulberry selection grown chiefly by fruit collectors for its notably large individual berries, which run bigger than most red mulberry seedlings even though the tree is not a particularly heavy or prolific bearer compared with more productive named cultivars. It grows into a substantial shade tree if left unpruned, so gardeners with limited space should prune regularly to keep it at a manageable home-orchard size. Fruit ripens over several weeks in early-to-midsummer and drops as it ripens, so a tarp or sheet spread beneath the canopy makes harvest far easier than hand-picking. Because named red mulberry selections like Johnson are propagated almost entirely by grafting or cuttings rather than seed, sourcing typically means ordering from specialty mulberry or fruit-collector nurseries rather than general garden centers.
sources: Growing Fruit forum (mulberry cultivar identification discussion)
North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox (Morus rubra)

common_name: Travis Mulberry (Texas Hill Country Red Mulberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in spring in full sun to partial shade on well-drained soil; Travis is a heat-tolerant Texas selection but can be difficult to source, so confirm availability with a specialty fruit-tree nursery before planning around it.

directions: Travis is a red mulberry selection originating in Travis County, Texas, regarded by fruit collectors as a superior-fruiting form of the species well adapted to hot, humid Gulf South and Texas summers. It produces good-flavored fruit typical of red mulberry over an extended early-summer harvest window, dropping ripe berries continuously, so a tarp beneath the canopy simplifies harvest. It grows into a large shade tree without regular pruning, so size control is an ongoing commitment in a home garden setting. Availability is limited compared with widely distributed cultivars like Illinois Everbearing, so sourcing typically requires a specialty native-plant or fruit-tree nursery rather than a general garden center.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox (Morus rubra 'Travis')

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Beautiful Day is self-fertile and its pale fruit will not stain hands, clothing, or patios the way dark-fruited mulberries do.

directions: Beautiful Day is a white-fruited mulberry selected for medium-small, sweet berries that ripen to a creamy white rather than staining dark red or black, making it a practical choice for planting near patios, driveways, or walkways where fruit drop from dark-fruited mulberries would otherwise cause a staining mess. Fruit ripens in late June and is well suited to fresh eating or drying, with a honeyed sweetness and relatively low acidity typical of white mulberry selections. The tree grows into a substantial rounded canopy with glossy leaves that turn gold in fall, so plan for a mature shade-tree size or commit to regular pruning if space is limited. As with other mulberries, harvest continues over several weeks as fruit ripens unevenly; shaking the tree over a tarp is an efficient way to collect a large crop.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Italian responds well to semi-annual pruning and can be kept to 15-20 feet instead of growing into a full-size shade tree.

directions: Italian is a white mulberry selection grown for large, abundant, dark black fruit with rich, sweet flavor, ripening among the earliest of the named mulberry cultivars, typically starting in mid-June and continuing into July. With training and semi-annual pruning it can be maintained at a manageable 15-20 feet rather than allowed to grow into a full-size shade tree, making it a practical home-orchard choice where space is limited. The heavy, early crop makes it a good companion planting alongside later-ripening mulberry cultivars to extend the harvest season. As with other dark-fruited mulberries, ripe berries drop continuously and will stain hands, clothing, and pavement, so harvest by shaking the tree over a tarp or sheet rather than hand-picking a large crop.
